## Summary

Executives at S&P 500 companies outside technology now talk about AI on most of their earnings calls. From July to September 2026 they did on 60.5% of calls, up from 32.1% in January to March 2024.

Few of them put a number on what it delivers. Last quarter an executive attached a figure to what AI saved, sped up or earned on 25 of 387 calls, 6.5%. That is up from 1.6% of calls in 2024, but it means that on about nine in ten calls where executives talked about AI, they gave no number for its payoff.

The numbers come from a small group. 86 companies have put a figure on AI at least once since January 2024, and nine of them, led by Airbnb and UnitedHealth, account for 47 of the 158 calls. The most common figure is a savings target for a company-wide cost program in which AI is one lever among several. The rest are narrow results in customer service, claims and document processing, and software development.

Analysts have started to ask. An analyst asked about AI savings, productivity or returns on 6.7% of calls last quarter, against about 1% in 2024, and on 15.1% of the first 86 calls of October.

## Abstract

We read the earnings calls of the companies in the S&P 500 outside the technology sector, 4,335 calls by 403 companies held from 1 January 2024 to 23 October 2026, using the speaker-by-speaker transcripts in the Equibles earnings call archive. We count a call as mentioning AI when an executive used the term, and as putting a number on AI when an executive attached a specific figure to what AI delivered: money saved, time or cost cut, a share of work automated, productivity, or revenue from AI products, achieved or targeted. Every candidate statement was read by hand.

The share of calls where executives mentioned AI rose from 32.1% in January to March 2024 to 60.5% in July to September 2026. The share where they put a number on it rose from 1.8% to 6.5%, or from 5.6% to 10.7% of the calls that mentioned AI. Financial services companies did both most often, mentioning AI on 89.1% of their calls in January to September 2026 and quantifying it on 11.4%. Energy and basic materials companies mentioned AI on 50% and 42% of their calls and never put a number on it. Of the 70 calls with a number in January to September 2026, 23 were company-wide savings or productivity programs, 17 back-office work such as claims and documents, 12 AI products and AI-assisted sales, 8 customer service, 7 software development and 3 product development.

## Twice the talk, a few more numbers

In early 2024 executives mentioned AI on about a third of non-tech calls. The share passed half in July to September 2025 and has held at about 60% for three quarters.

Calls where an executive put a figure on what AI delivered grew faster, from a low base. They went from 1.8% of calls in January to March 2024 to 6.5% in July to September 2026, with the steepest rise in the second half of 2025.

October covers the first 86 calls of the reporting season, mostly banks and other financial companies, so its share is not comparable with a full quarter.

Early examples were rare and specific. On Walmart (WMT $120.29 +0.33% ) 's August 2024 call , the chief executive said the company had used large language models to create or improve over 850 million pieces of data in its product catalog.

> “Without the use of generative AI, this work would have required nearly 100 times the current headcount to complete in the same amount of time.” Doug McMillon, chief executive, Walmart, earnings call, 15 August 2024

## Who puts a number on it

In January to September 2026, executives at 316 of the 399 non-tech companies in the sample talked about AI on at least one call. Executives at 49 of them put a number on what it delivered.

The same companies come back quarter after quarter. Airbnb (ABNB $171.05 -0.56% ) and UnitedHealth (UNH $410.70 -1.77% ) gave a figure on six of their calls since January 2024, and Nasdaq (NDAQ $104.72 +2.11% ) , C.H. Robinson (CHRW $140.15 -0.72% ) , Expedia (EXPE $283.97 -1.74% ) , FactSet (FDS $323.39 -2.39% ) , Global Payments (GPN $81.86 -1.16% ) , Equifax (EFX $178.56 -2.08% ) and WTW (WTW $324.67 -0.10% ) on five each. Those nine companies account for 47 of the 158 calls with a number.

Financial services companies, banks, insurers, exchanges, card networks and data providers, talk about AI on almost every call and quantify it most often. Energy and basic materials companies talked about AI on 50% and 42% of their calls, often as a source of demand for power, gas or materials, but none put a number on what AI did for their own operations.

## Where the numbers come from

The largest group is a savings or productivity target for the whole company, with AI named as a driver. WTW tied a new program directly to AI on its July 2026 call .

We expect to capture efficiencies and generate approximately $400 million in run rate savings through an investment of approximately $625 million, reflecting a disciplined cash cost to achieve ratio of about 1.6.” Carl Hess, chief executive, WTW, earnings call, 30 July 2026

Many of these targets credit AI alongside other levers, such as reorganizations, procurement or offshoring, so the figure is not AI's alone. Of the 25 calls with a number last quarter, 19 credited the figure to AI alone, and 6 named AI as one of several drivers.
